problem: Hedge lost: source says some few MAY modify the convictions of all; candidate states it flatly.
replacement: [Footnote a: If I ask which state of society is most favorable to the great revolutions of the mind, I find that it lies somewhere between the complete equality of the whole community and the absolute separation of ranks. Under a system of castes, generations succeed one another without altering men’s positions; some have nothing more, others nothing better, to hope for. The imagination slumbers in this universal silence and stillness, and the very idea of change fades from the human mind. When ranks have been abolished and social conditions are almost equalized, all men are in ceaseless excitement, but each stands alone, independent and weak. This latter state of things is extremely different from the former, yet it has one point in common: great revolutions of the human mind seldom occur in it. But between these two extremes in the history of nations there is an intermediate period, as glorious as it is turbulent. In it the conditions of men are not settled enough for the mind to be lulled into torpor, yet they are unequal enough for men to exercise a vast power over one another’s minds, and a few may modify the convictions of all. It is at such times that great reformers start up and new opinions suddenly change the face of the world.]
